legal.headline: When a child breaks the law, the law must not break the child: Supreme Court Justice BV Nagarathna
legal.hook: When a child breaks the law, the law must not break the child: Supreme Court Justice BV Nagarathna
legal.summary: In a recent ruling, the Supreme Court of India, led by Justice BV Nagarathna, emphasized the need for a child-friendly approach in the justice system, particularly when minors are involved in criminal activities. The case in question involved a 16-year-old boy accused of theft, whose bail application was denied by the High Court. Justice Nagarathna highlighted that the law should not impose harsh penalties on children, stating, 'When a child breaks the law, the law must not break the child.' The court underscored the importance of rehabilitation over punishment, referencing the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015. The Supreme Court ultimately granted bail to the minor, directing that he be released into the care of his parents. This decision reflects a broader judicial trend towards prioritizing the welfare of children in legal proceedings.
legal.contextNote: The ruling is grounded in the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, particularly sections concerning the treatment of minors in conflict with the law. (1) In-house counsel should review their organization's policies on interactions with minors, ensuring compliance with child protection laws. legal.hook: SCBA informs the revised arrangement of Cause List, to be published in 2 parts, ending the practice of assigning a sequence to matters at 10:30 a.m

This change, communicated by the Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA), aims to enhance the management of court schedules by placing fresh and early-hearing matters in Part A of the cause list, while matters that have already been noticed will be included in Part B. This new sequencing ends the previous practice of assigning a sequence to matters at 10:30 a.m., which was often criticized for causing delays and inefficiencies in court proceedings. The SCBA's announcement signals a shift towards a more organized approach to case management, although specific implementation details and the timeline for this change have not been disclosed.

As a result, the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) has decided to relocate the President's Trophy matches that were initially scheduled in these cities. The PCB has not yet announced the new venues for the matches, but they are expected to be shifted to safer locations to ensure the safety of players and officials.
